title: How do you read stacked bar charts without missing the real story?
description: How to read stacked and 100% stacked bar charts in case interviews, avoid the classic misreadings, and find the segment that changed, with a worked example.
hook: Read a stacked bar chart by first checking whether it shows totals or shares, then comparing the totals, then working out each segment's size by subtraction rather than by eye. The real story is usually which segment is driving the change, and that is exactly what a stacked chart makes easy to miss.
body:
Two kinds of stacked bar

  • Stacked bars show totals split into segments. Bar height is the total; each coloured block is one part of it.
  • 100% stacked bars show only each segment's share. Every bar is the same height, so you cannot see whether the total grew or shrank.

Spotting which one you have is the first job, because the same picture means very different things in each.

How to read one quickly

  1. Check whether it shows totals or shares. Look at the axis: dollars or percent?
  2. Compare the totals first. How much did the whole grow or shrink?
  3. Read the bottom segment directly. It sits on the axis, so it is easy to compare across bars.
  4. Calculate the others. Middle and top segments float, so work out each one's size by subtracting its bottom edge from its top edge rather than guessing.
  5. Find the segment driving the change, then say what it means and what to look at next.

A worked example

A chart shows a retailer's revenue by channel over two years:

ChannelYear 1Year 2Change
Stores$75M$150M+100%
Online$40M$36M−10%
Wholesale$90M$99M+10%
Total$205M$285M+39%

Total revenue grew by $80M. Stores contributed $75M of that, about 94% of the growth. Online shrank.

Strong: "Revenue grew 39%, but almost all of it came from stores, which doubled. Online actually fell 10%, which is a worrying sign if the client is investing in digital. I'd want to know whether the store growth came from new openings or from existing stores."
Weak: "Stores went from 75 to 150, online from 40 to 36, and wholesale from 90 to 99."

Now look at shares. Wholesale fell from 44% of revenue to 35%, even though it grew by 10% in dollars. On a 100% stacked version of this chart, wholesale would look like a business in decline. It is not; it is just growing more slowly than stores.

A shrinking share can hide growth

This is the classic trap with 100% stacked charts. Suppose a company has $60M of store revenue and $40M online in year one ($100M total), then $60M of each in year two ($120M total). Online's share rises from 40% to 50%, and stores' share falls from 60% to 50%.

A 100% stacked chart would show stores losing ten points of share. It would not show that store revenue was flat, or that total revenue rose by $20M. Never say a segment's sales fell just because its share got smaller. Ask for the totals.

Mix changes move margins

A changing mix matters most when segments earn different margins. In the example above, suppose stores earn a 20% margin and online 10%, because of delivery and returns. Year one profit is $12M + $4M = $16M, a 16% margin. Year two profit is $12M + $6M = $18M, a 15% margin. Profit grew, but the margin fell, purely because of mix.

That is often the real insight: "The business grew 20%, but all the growth came from the lower-margin channel. Before calling this good growth, I'd compare contribution margins by channel." Weighted averages explains the arithmetic behind mix effects.

Common traps

  • Reading share as value. On a 100% chart, a falling share can mean a growing segment.
  • Guessing middle segments by eye. Calculate them from the gridlines.
  • Describing the parts and missing the total. Always start with the total change.
  • Ignoring margin differences between segments when the mix shifts.

Practice

1. A 100% stacked chart shows a product's share of a category falling from 30% to 25%. The category grew from $200M to $300M. Did the product's sales fall?

Show the answer

No. Sales went from 30% × $200M = $60M to 25% × $300M = $75M, a 25% increase. It lost share in a fast-growing market. The question for the client is why it grew more slowly than competitors, not why it shrank.

2. Using the channel table above, what was online's share of revenue in each year?

Show the answer

Year 1: $40M ÷ $205M = 19.5%. Year 2: $36M ÷ $285M = 12.6%. Online lost about seven points of share, partly because it shrank and partly because stores grew so fast.
